title: Audio Shifting Adjustable
rawBody:
Audio shifting designed to create a perception of motion can be paused or turned off.


:::applies-when
- content includes audio shifting.
:::

:::except-when
- operating system or user agent triggers audio shifting.
:::

appliesWhen: • content includes audio shifting.
exceptWhen: • operating system or user agent triggers audio shifting.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For audio shifting caused by the digital content (in contrast to the operating system or user agent):

  1. Check that there is a setting to pause or turn off the audio shifting.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.
derived.methods: • Add a setting to pause audio shifting or turn it off.

plainEnglish.summary: Audio Shifting Adjustable: Audio shifting designed to create a perception of motion can be paused or turned off.

title: Haptic Stimulation Adjustable
rawBody:
Haptic feedback can be reduced or turned off.


:::applies-when
- content triggers haptic feedback.
:::

:::except-when
- the operating system or user agent converts non-haptic feedback to haptics at user request.
:::

appliesWhen: • content triggers haptic feedback.
exceptWhen: • the operating system or user agent converts non-haptic feedback to haptics at user request.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For haptic feedback caused by the digital content (in contrast to the operating system or user agent).

  1. Check if there is a setting that allows for reducing or turning off the haptic feedback.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.
derived.methods: • Add a setting to reduce haptic feedback or turn it off.

plainEnglish.summary: Haptic Stimulation Adjustable: Haptic feedback can be reduced or turned off.

title: No flashing over threshold (no exceptions)
rawBody:
Flashes are below the general flash and red flash thresholds without a minimum size.

:::applies-when
- Content includes flashes.
:::

:::note
Avoiding flashing entirely is the safest option because some people who may not know they are susceptible to photosensitive seizures, and some people may have a much larger view of content than the default (zoomed in or with the display close to the eye).
:::

appliesWhen: • Content includes flashes.
notes: Avoiding flashing entirely is the safest option because some people who may not know they are susceptible to photosensitive seizures, and some people may have a much larger view of content than the default (zoomed in or with the display close to the eye).
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each instance of flashing:

  1. Check that the flashing is below the size threshold defined by the general flash and red flash thresholds.
  2. Check that the flashing is below the frequency defined by the general flash and red flash thresholds.

Expected results

  • #1 or #2 is true.
derived.methods: • Design content without using flashing.

plainEnglish.summary: No flashing over threshold (no exceptions): Flashes are below the general flash and red flash thresholds without a minimum size.

title: No Flashing Over Threshold
rawBody:
Flashes are below the general flash and red flash thresholds.

:::applies-when
- Content includes flashes.
:::

:::except-when
- The flashing is essential.
:::

:::note
If there is an accessibility supported method of setting a user-preference to prevent flashing, the content can be considered to avoid flashing if that preference is respected.
:::

:::ednote
There is research into the size and frequency metrics underway. The exact values are likely to change before WCAG3 is published.
:::

appliesWhen: • Content includes flashes.
exceptWhen: • The flashing is essential.
notes: If there is an accessibility supported method of setting a user-preference to prevent flashing, the content can be considered to avoid flashing if that preference is respected.
editorNotes: There is research into the size and frequency metrics underway. The exact values are likely to change before WCAG3 is published.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each instance of flashing:

  1. Check if the flashing is essential.
  2. Check that the flashing is below the thresholds defined by the general flash and red flash thresholds.

Expected results

  • #1 or #2 is true.
derived.methods:
• Consider if flashing is essential and, if it is not, remove it.
  • Ensure that an accessibility supported user setting to avoid animation and flashing is respected.
  • Ensure that any flashing is below [X] size in the users’ view.
derived.intent:
Some people with seizure disorders can have a seizure triggered by flashing visual content. Most people are unaware that they have this disorder until it strikes. In 1997, a cartoon on television in Japan sent over 700 children to the hospital, including about 500 who had seizures. Warnings do not work well because they are often missed, especially by children who may not be able to read them.

The objective of this requirement is to ensure that content avoids the types of flash that are most likely to cause seizures when viewed even for a second.

plainEnglish.summary: No Flashing Over Threshold: Flashes are below the general flash and red flash thresholds.

title: No visual motion (no exceptions)
rawBody: Content does not include pseudo-motion or visual motion lasting longer than 5 seconds.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each page/view:

  1. Check if content includes visual motion or pseudo-motion.

Expected results

  • #1 is false.
derived.methods: • Design content without using visual motion or pseudo-motion.

plainEnglish.summary: No visual motion (no exceptions): Content does not include pseudo-motion or visual motion lasting longer than 5 seconds.

title: No Visual Motion
rawBody:
Content does not include pseudo-motion or visual motion lasting longer than 5 seconds.

:::except-when
- The motion or pseudo-motion is essential.
:::

exceptWhen: • The motion or pseudo-motion is essential.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each page/view:

  1. Check if content includes visual motion or pseudo-motion.
  2. For each instance, check that the visual motion or pseudo-motion is essential.

Expected results

  • #1 is false, or
  • #2 is true.
derived.methods: • Consider if motion or pseudo-motion is essential, and if it is not, refrain from including it.

plainEnglish.summary: No Visual Motion: Content does not include pseudo-motion or visual motion lasting longer than 5 seconds.

title: Safe Content Review
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:  

* We have reviewed content for violent, explicit, or troubling content and provided appropriate warnings before accessing the content. 

::assertion-required

- title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
- date of when the review was conducted
- date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)

:::note
Troubling content will vary based on culture or individual situations, and reviews should take target audiences into consideration.
:::

notes: Troubling content will vary based on culture or individual situations, and reviews should take target audiences into consideration.

plainEnglish.summary:
Safe Content Review: [Title, role, or organization] asserts that:  

 We have reviewed content for violent, explicit, or troubling content and provided appropriate warnings before accessing the content.

title: Single Flash
rawBody:
Content does not include a change of contrast (over 4.5:1) going from light to dark (or dark to light) of more than 30% of the visible content area (viewport).

:::except-when
- A new page/view is loaded.
- The flash is essential.
:::


:::ednote
This is a new provision for a big, intense, single on/off flash. This is reported as a trigger by group members, but we need data on this, and a definition that includes size/intensity to avoid including non-triggers such as menus.
:::

:::ednote 
This provision relies on the color contrast algorithm in WCAG 2. When the algorithm is updated for WCAG 3, the contrast metric will also be updated.
:::

exceptWhen:
• A new page/view is loaded.
  • The flash is essential.
editorNotes: This is a new provision for a big, intense, single on/off flash. This is reported as a trigger by group members, but we need data on this, and a definition that includes size/intensity to avoid including non-triggers such as menus.
This provision relies on the color contrast algorithm in WCAG 2. When the algorithm is updated for WCAG 3, the contrast metric will also be updated.
derived.tests:
For each change of contrast:

  1. Check if the change of contrast is triggered by a loading a new page/view.
  2. Check that the change of contrast is less than 4.5:1.
  3. Check that the area of the change of contrast is less than 30% of the viewport.

Expected results

#1, #2, or #3 is true.
derived.methods: • Design content without large changes of contrast. For example, when a menu with a light background is opened, it opens over a light background. Videos do not go from a dark to light background in less than a second.

plainEnglish.summary: Single Flash: Content does not include a change of contrast (over 4.5:1) going from light to dark (or dark to light) of more than 30% of the visible content area (viewport).

title: Trigger Warning Available
rawBody:
A warning is provided before users encounter triggers and a mechanism is available to access the same information without the triggering content.

:::applies-when
- triggers are present.
:::

:::note
Triggers are flashing, motion lasting more than 5 seconds, and pseudo-motion.
:::

appliesWhen: • triggers are present.
notes: Triggers are flashing, motion lasting more than 5 seconds, and pseudo-motion.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each trigger:

  1. Check if a warning is provided before the user encounters the trigger.
  2. Check that the same information is available without triggers.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.
derived.methods: • Provide a warning for triggers and provide an option without the triggers.

plainEnglish.summary: Trigger Warning Available: A warning is provided before users encounter triggers and a mechanism is available to access the same information without the triggering content.

title: Visual Stimulation
rawBody: Visual stimulation from combinations of density, color, movement, etc. can be reduced or turned off.

plainEnglish.summary: Visual Stimulation: Visual stimulation from combinations of density, color, movement, etc.

title: Consistent Navigation Labels
rawBody:
The labeling of navigation items within blocks of navigation that are repeated on multiple pages/views in the conformance scope or process is consistent.

:::except-when
* Labels for navigation items that are marked as 'current' within the conformance scope or process.
:::

:::ednote
This relates to consistency and terminology within blocks of navigation. The consistent ordering of blocks of navigation within a page/view is covered by 'Consistent relative order'.
:::

exceptWhen: • Labels for navigation items that are marked as ‘current’ within the conformance scope or process.
editorNotes: This relates to consistency and terminology within blocks of navigation. The consistent ordering of blocks of navigation within a page/view is covered by ‘Consistent relative order’.
derived.tests:
Consistent main navigation labels

Procedure

For each repeated block of navigation across multiple pages/views of the conformance scope or process:

  1. The navigation items within each block of navigation have the same names across all pages/views of the conformance scope or process.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.
derived.intent:
The intent of this success criterion is to ensure consistent identification of functional components that appear repeatedly within a set of web pages. A strategy that people who use screen readers use when operating a website is to rely heavily on their familiarity with functions that may appear on different web pages. If identical functions have different labels (or, more generally, a different accessible name) on different web pages, the site will be considerably more difficult to use. It may also be confusing and increase the cognitive load for people with cognitive limitations. Therefore, consistent labeling will help.

This consistency extends to the text alternatives. If icons or other non-text items have the same functionality, then their text alternatives should be consistent as well.

If there are two components on a web page that both have the same functionality as a component on another page in a set of web pages, then all 3 must be consistent. Hence the two on the same page will be consistent.

While it is desirable and recommended practice always to be consistent within a single web page, 3.2.4 Consistent Identification only addresses consistency within a set of web pages where something is repeated on more than one page in the set.

plainEnglish.summary: Consistent Navigation Labels: The labeling of navigation items within blocks of navigation that are repeated on multiple pages/views in the conformance scope or process is consistent.

title: Consistent Navigation Order
rawBody:
The relative order of navigation items is consistent within blocks of navigation that are repeated on multiple pages/views of the conformance scope or process.

:::applies-when
- In a set of pages/views.
:::

:::ednote
This relates to consistency and terminology within blocks of navigation. The consistent ordering of blocks of navigation within a page/view is covered by 'Consistent relative order'.
:::

appliesWhen: • In a set of pages/views.
editorNotes: This relates to consistency and terminology within blocks of navigation. The consistent ordering of blocks of navigation within a page/view is covered by ‘Consistent relative order’.
derived.tests:
Consistent main navigation relative order

Procedure

For each repeated blocks of navigation across multiple pages/views of the conformance scope or process:

  1. The navigation items within each block of navigation have the same relative order across all pages/views of the conformance scope or process.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.
derived.intent:
The intent of this success criterion is to encourage the use of consistent visual layout and source order for users who interact with repeated content within a set of web pages and need to locate specific information or functionality more than once.

Individuals with low vision who use screen magnification to display a small portion of the screen at a time often use visual cues and page boundaries to quickly locate repeated content. Presenting repeated content in the same order is also important for visual users who use spatial memory or visual cues within the design to locate repeated content.

Likewise, users who are blind and navigate through content on pages sequentially benefit from having navigational mechanisms occur in a consistent order relative to the overall source order and structure of the page.

It is important to note that the use of the phrase “same order” in this section is not meant to imply that sub-navigation menus cannot be used or that blocks of secondary navigation or page structure cannot be used. Instead, this success criterion is intended to assist users who interact with repeated content across web pages to be able to predict the location of the content they are looking for and find it more quickly when they encounter it again.

Users may initiate a change in the order by using adaptive user agents or by setting preferences so that the information is presented in a way that is most useful to them.

plainEnglish.summary: Consistent Navigation Order: The relative order of navigation items is consistent within blocks of navigation that are repeated on multiple pages/views of the conformance scope or process.

title: Consistent Structural Order
rawBody:
The relative order of structural components remains consistent throughout each variation of pages/views in the conformance scope.

:::applies-when
- In a set of pages/views.
:::

:::note
Relative order means that content can be added or removed, but repeated items are in the same order relative to each other.
:::

appliesWhen: • In a set of pages/views.
notes: Relative order means that content can be added or removed, but repeated items are in the same order relative to each other.
derived.tests:
Consistent relative order for website

Procedure

For each variation of pages/views in the conformance scope:

  1. Identify common structural components across multiple pages/views.
  2. Check that components are presented in the same order within each page/view.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Consistent Structural Order: The relative order of structural components remains consistent throughout each variation of pages/views in the conformance scope.

title: Error Messages Collocated
rawBody:
Error messages are visually collocated with the error source or the focus is moved to the error message and a mechanism is available to move to the input that is in error. 

:::applies-when
- Error messages relate to user input.
:::

appliesWhen: • Error messages relate to user input.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each page/view:

  1. Zoom in 400%.
  2. Trigger errors.
  3. Check that the error is visible next to the trigger or that the focus moves to the error.

Expected results

  • #3 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Error Messages Collocated: Error messages are visually collocated with the error source or the focus is moved to the error message and a mechanism is available to move to the input that is in error.

title: Error Messages Persistent
rawBody: Error messages persist at least until the error is resolved or the user dismisses them.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each error message:

  1. Check that the error message persists until the user fixes the error or dismisses the message.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.
derived.methods:
• Keep track of the state of the error and make visibility of the error message depending on this state.
  • In a form, revalidate all fields when the form is submitted and remove all error messages that are no longer relevant.
  • Add a “Dismiss” button to the error that makes the error message disappear.

plainEnglish.summary: Error Messages Persistent: Error messages persist at least until the error is resolved or the user dismisses them.

title: Error Notifications Available
rawBody:
Errors that are programmatically determined are identified and the problem is described to the user in text.

:::example
- invalid form input
- server errors
- application errors
:::

examples:
• invalid form input
  • server errors
  • application errors
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each page/view:

  1. Trigger errors.
  2. For each error, check that the nature of the problem is identified and described.

Expected results

  • #2 is true for each error.

plainEnglish.summary: Error Notifications Available: Errors that are programmatically determined are identified and the problem is described to the user in text.

title: Error Suggestions Provided
rawBody:
Error messages include suggestions for corrections.

:::applies-when
- Errors require corrections by the user.
:::

:::except-when
- including suggestions would jeopardize the security or purpose of the content.
:::

appliesWhen: • Errors require corrections by the user.
exceptWhen: • including suggestions would jeopardize the security or purpose of the content.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each error message:

  1. Check that the error needs correction by the user.
  2. Check that the error message includes suggestions for how to fix the error.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: Error Suggestions Provided: Error messages include suggestions for corrections.

title: Errors Associated
rawBody:
When input validation fails, the errors are visually and programmatically associated with the element that caused the error or that can resolve it.

:::example
Failing validation includes but is not limited to:

- when input is required and the field is left empty
- when the user input does not meet the requested format
:::

examples:
Failing validation includes but is not limited to:

  • when input is required and the field is left empty
  • when the user input does not meet the requested format
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each validation error:

  1. Check that the validation error is indicated visually.
  2. Check that the validation error is indicated programmatically.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: Errors Associated: When input validation fails, the errors are visually and programmatically associated with the element that caused the error or that can resolve it.

title: Errors Indicated In Multiple Ways
rawBody:
Error messages are visually indicated using at least two of the following:

* a symbol that is consistent throughout the conformance scope
* color that differentiates the error message from surrounding content
* a textual indication

:::example
An example of a "textual indication" would be to add  "Error: " before the error description.
:::

examples: An example of a “textual indication” would be to add “Error: ” before the error description.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each validation error:

  1. Check that it meets at least two of the listed indicators (symbol, color, or text).

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary:
Errors Indicated In Multiple Ways: Error messages are visually indicated using at least two of the following:

 a symbol that is consistent throughout the conformance scope
 color that differentiates the error message from surrounding content
 a textual indication

title: Data Entry Validated
rawBody:
Data entered is validated after the user enters data, either:

* when the user leaves the field, or 
* when the form is submitted

derived.tests:
Procedure

  1. Check that no validation has not occurred before data entry.
  2. Enter data.
  3. Check that validation is provided immediately after data entry or occurs before submission.

Expected results

  • #1 and #3 are true.

plainEnglish.summary:
Data Entry Validated: Data entered is validated after the user enters data, either:

 when the user leaves the field, or 
 when the form is submitted

title: Error Prevention Review
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that: 

* For each form in the conformance claim, we have reviewed the form designs to reduce the possibility of users making mistakes. 

This review includes checking to make sure that we:

* Make the user enter as little information as possible.
* Clearly indicate required fields.
* For long numbers, divide input fields into chunks (supporting autocomplete across fields).
* Use an interface where only valid input can be selected.
* Use autocomplete and personalization of form controls.
* Use common words and metrics or units that users are likely to be familiar with.
* Automatically correct input errors when possible and reliable.
* Provide the user with known suggestions and corrections.

::assertion-required

* title, role, or organization making the assertion
* date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)

::assertion-recommended

* documentation of which forms were reviewed
* documentation of any changes made as a result of the review
* date of usability testing, if applicable

plainEnglish.summary:
Error Prevention Review: [Title, role, or organization] asserts that: 

 For each form in the conformance claim, we have reviewed the form designs to reduce the possibility of users making mistakes.

title: Errors Preventable
rawBody:
Data entry interfaces allow for users to do at least one of the following before submission:

* Review, confirm, and correct all information.
* Review and correct input errors found during validation.

:::except-when
- entered data is auto-saved and/or reversible.
:::

:::ednote
Editors are looking at removing the grey area that may exist in this requirement due to interpretations of the word “submission“ (pressing “Submit” in the UI or receiving information server-side).
:::

exceptWhen: • entered data is auto-saved and/or reversible.
editorNotes: Editors are looking at removing the grey area that may exist in this requirement due to interpretations of the word “submission“ (pressing “Submit” in the UI or receiving information server-side).
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each data entry point:

  1. Check that users can return at any point in the process to correct data they entered.
  2. If it’s not possible to go back and correct the data during the process, check that the information being submitted can be reviewed and corrected before submission, or that it’s validated and can be fixed before submission.

Expected results

  • #1 or #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary:
Errors Preventable: Data entry interfaces allow for users to do at least one of the following before submission:

 Review, confirm, and correct all information.

title: Submission Status Notified
rawBody:
Data entry interfaces notify users of submission status at the time of submission.

:::applies-when
- data submission has succeeded or failed.
:::

appliesWhen: • data submission has succeeded or failed.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each data submission:

  1. Check that the user is notified about the submission immediately afterwards.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Submission Status Notified: Data entry interfaces notify users of submission status at the time of submission.

title: Feedback Mechanism Available
rawBody: A mechanism is available to provide feedback to authors.

derived.tests:
Procedure

Within the conformance scope:

  1. Check that a feedback mechanism exists.
  2. Check that the feedback is sent to authors.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: Feedback Mechanism Available: A mechanism is available to provide feedback to authors.

title: Consistent Help Available
rawBody:
Help is labeled consistently and is available in a consistent location relative to other content.

:::applies-when
* human contact information, a human contact mechanism, a self-help option, or a fully automated contact mechanism is available.
:::

appliesWhen: • human contact information, a human contact mechanism, a self-help option, or a fully automated contact mechanism is available.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each help item in a page / view:

  1. Check that it is labeled consistently.
  2. Check that it remains in the same relative visual and programmatic location.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: Consistent Help Available: Help is labeled consistently and is available in a consistent location relative to other content.

title: Contextual Help Available
rawBody: Context-sensitive help is available.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each interactive element:

  1. Check for potentially confusing or difficult interactions such as formatting restrictions or interdependencies.
  2. For any element identified in #1, check that context-sensitive help is available.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Contextual Help Available: Context-sensitive help is available.

title: Conversational Support Available
rawBody: Conversational support allowing both text and speech formats is available.

derived.tests:
Procedure

  1. Check that a conversational support mechanism is available.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Conversational Support Available: Conversational support allowing both text and speech formats is available.

title: Data Visualizations
rawBody:
:::ednote
Editors are considering removal of this requirement.
:::

Help is available to understand and use data visualizations.

editorNotes: Editors are considering removal of this requirement.

plainEnglish.summary: Data Visualizations: Help is available to understand and use data visualizations.

title: Disabled Controls Explained
rawBody:
Information explaining why a visible interactive element is disabled is available and, if the user can take action(s) to enable the element, those action(s) are described.

:::example
When a submit button is disabled until all required fields are filled in, explain that this is the case.
:::

examples: When a submit button is disabled until all required fields are filled in, explain that this is the case.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each visible disabled control:

  1. Check that instructions are available that explain how to enable it.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Disabled Controls Explained: Information explaining why a visible interactive element is disabled is available and, if the user can take action(s) to enable the element, those action(s) are described.

title: Help Usability Testing
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

* Help and training was added based on usability testing with people with cognitive and mental health disabilities to identify gaps.

::assertion-required

* title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
* date of when the usability testing was conducted
* date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)

::assertion-recommended

* usability findings
* solutions added

:::example
Solutions include help with completing functionality such as data entry, task completion, search, and understanding complex ideas and visualizations.
:::

examples: Solutions include help with completing functionality such as data entry, task completion, search, and understanding complex ideas and visualizations.

plainEnglish.summary:
Help Usability Testing: [Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

 Help and training was added based on usability testing with people with cognitive and mental health disabilities to identify gaps.

title: New Interfaces
rawBody:
A mechanism to learn a new interface or revert to the older design is available.

:::applies-when
- Interfaces dramatically change due to redesign.
:::

:::except-when
- The new interface is essential.
:::

appliesWhen: • Interfaces dramatically change due to redesign.
exceptWhen: • The new interface is essential.
derived.tests:
Procedure

  1. When an interface has been redesigned, check that a tutorial is available or that the user is given an opportunity to revert to the previous design.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: New Interfaces: A mechanism to learn a new interface or revert to the older design is available.

title: Personalizable Help
rawBody:
:::ednote
Editors are considering removal of this requirement.
:::

Help is adaptable and personalizable.

editorNotes: Editors are considering removal of this requirement.

plainEnglish.summary: Personalizable Help: Help is adaptable and personalizable.

title: Sensory Characteristics Not Relied On
rawBody:
Instructions and help do not rely on sensory characteristics.

:::example
Sensory characteristics include but are not limited to shape, color, size, visual location, orientation, or sound.
:::

examples: Sensory characteristics include but are not limited to shape, color, size, visual location, orientation, or sound.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each reference to shape, size, or position of an object:

  1. Check that the reference includes additional information that allows the item to be located and identified without any knowledge of its shape, size, or relative position.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Sensory Characteristics Not Relied On: Instructions and help do not rely on sensory characteristics.

title: Support Available
rawBody:
Support is available during data entry, task completion and search.

:::except-when
- the content does not include one or more of the mentioned processes.
:::

:::example
When the content does not include search, there is no requirement for support to be available for search.
:::

exceptWhen: • the content does not include one or more of the mentioned processes.
examples: When the content does not include search, there is no requirement for support to be available for search.

plainEnglish.summary: Support Available: Support is available during data entry, task completion and search.

title: Supported decision-making review
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

* We have conducted a review to identify when users need to make substantial decisions about money, privacy, or well-being. In these situations, additional support was provided, such as:
  * a clear layout of options advantages and disadvantages
  * aids for comprehension such as icons and graphics
  * reduced distractions

::assertion-required

* title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
* date of when the policy was implemented
* date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)

::assertion-recommended

* results of review
* documentation of decisions and changes made as a result

plainEnglish.summary:
Supported decision-making review: [Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

 We have conducted a review to identify when users need to make substantial decisions about money, privacy, or well-being.

title: Accessible Audio Player Selected
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

* We provide an audio player that supports appropriate media alternatives. The audio player includes the following features [list all that apply]:
  * turning audio descriptions on and off
  * changing the language of the audio descriptions

:::applies-when
- an audio format is used that does not play in standard browsers.
:::

::assertion-required

* title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
* date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)

For each audio and video player where sign language is not hard-coded:

exceptWhen: • Full or gross body movement is essential to the functionality.
notes: This includes both detection of body movement and actions to the device, such as shaking, that require body movement.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each instance of functionality that uses body movement:

  1. Check that the body movement is not the only way to achieve any functionality.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Body Movements Not Relied On: Functionality does not rely solely on full or gross body movement.

title: Eye Tracking Not Relied On
rawBody:
Content and functionality does not rely solely on eye tracking.

:::except-when
- Eye tracking is essential. 
:::

:::note
This is primarily aimed at ensuring there is an alternative for people who cannot use eye tracking (but do have sight) due to eye conditions.
:::

:::note
Some platforms may only allow eye tracking. Ideally the platforms allow additional mechanisms for control. 
:::

exceptWhen: • Eye tracking is essential.
notes: This is primarily aimed at ensuring there is an alternative for people who cannot use eye tracking (but do have sight) due to eye conditions.
Some platforms may only allow eye tracking. Ideally the platforms allow additional mechanisms for control.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For platforms that use eye-tracking for pointer use:

  1. Check that an alternative, such as using a switch control, is available.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Eye Tracking Not Relied On: Content and functionality does not rely solely on eye tracking.

title: Hover Content Persistent
rawBody:
If pointer hover can trigger content, then the pointer can be moved over the additional content without the additional content disappearing.

:::applies-when
- Receiving and then removing pointer hover or keyboard focus triggers additional content to become visible and then hidden, and the visual presentation of the additional content is controlled by the author and not by the user agent.
:::

:::note
This applies to content that appears in addition to the triggering of the interactive element itself. Since hidden interactive elements that are made visible on keyboard focus (such as links used to skip to another part of a page/view) do not present additional content, they are not covered by this requirement.
:::

:::example
Additional content controlled by the user agent includes browser tooltips created through use of the HTML `title` attribute.
:::

:::example
Custom tooltips, sub-menus, and other non-modal popups that display on hover and keyboard focus.
:::

appliesWhen: • Receiving and then removing pointer hover or keyboard focus triggers additional content to become visible and then hidden, and the visual presentation of the additional content is controlled by the author and not by the user agent.
notes: This applies to content that appears in addition to the triggering of the interactive element itself. Since hidden interactive elements that are made visible on keyboard focus (such as links used to skip to another part of a page/view) do not present additional content, they are not covered by this requirement.
examples: Additional content controlled by the user agent includes browser tooltips created through use of the HTML title attribute.
Custom tooltips, sub-menus, and other non-modal popups that display on hover and keyboard focus.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For additional content that appears on hover:

  1. Check that the pointer can be moved over the additional content without the additional content disappearing.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Hover Content Persistent: If pointer hover can trigger content, then the pointer can be moved over the additional content without the additional content disappearing.

title: Hover Or Focus Content Dismissible
rawBody:
A mechanism is available to dismiss content that appears on pointer hover or keyboard focus without moving pointer hover or keyboard focus, unless the additional content does not obscure or replace other content.

:::applies-when
- Receiving and then removing pointer hover or keyboard focus triggers additional content to become visible and then hidden, and the visual presentation of the additional content is controlled by the author and not by the user agent.
:::

:::note
This applies to content that appears in addition to the triggering of the interactive element itself. Since hidden interactive elements that are made visible on keyboard focus (such as links used to skip to another part of a page/view) do not present additional content, they are not covered by this requirement.
:::

:::example
Additional content controlled by the user agent includes browser tooltips created through use of the HTML `title` attribute.
:::

:::example
Custom tooltips, sub-menus, and other non-modal popups that display on hover and keyboard focus.
:::

appliesWhen: • Receiving and then removing pointer hover or keyboard focus triggers additional content to become visible and then hidden, and the visual presentation of the additional content is controlled by the author and not by the user agent.
notes: This applies to content that appears in addition to the triggering of the interactive element itself. Since hidden interactive elements that are made visible on keyboard focus (such as links used to skip to another part of a page/view) do not present additional content, they are not covered by this requirement.
examples: Additional content controlled by the user agent includes browser tooltips created through use of the HTML title attribute.
Custom tooltips, sub-menus, and other non-modal popups that display on hover and keyboard focus.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For additional content that appears on hover:

  1. Check that the content can be closed without moving the pointer way from the trigger. Either by pressing Esc, by pressing another documented keyboard shortcut, or by activating the trigger.

For additional content that appears on focus:

  1. Check that the content can be closed without moving the focus away from the trigger. Either by pressing Esc, by pressing another other documented keyboard shortcut, or by activating the trigger.

Expected results

  • For additional content that appears on hover: #1 is true.
  • For additional content that appears on focus: #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Hover Or Focus Content Dismissible: A mechanism is available to dismiss content that appears on pointer hover or keyboard focus without moving pointer hover or keyboard focus, unless the additional content does not obscure or replace other content.

title: Hover Or Focus Content Persistent
rawBody:
Content that appears on pointer hover or keyboard focus remains visible until the hover or keyboard focus trigger is removed, the user dismisses it, or its information is no longer valid.

:::applies-when
- Receiving and then removing pointer hover or keyboard focus triggers additional content to become visible and then hidden, and the visual presentation of the additional content is controlled by the author and not by the user agent.
:::

:::note
This applies to content that appears in addition to the triggering of the interactive element itself. Since hidden interactive elements that are made visible on keyboard focus (such as links used to skip to another part of a page/view) do not present additional content, they are not covered by this requirement.
:::

:::example
Additional content controlled by the user agent includes browser tooltips created through use of the HTML `title` attribute.
:::

:::example
Custom tooltips, sub-menus, and other non-modal popups that display on hover and keyboard focus.
:::

appliesWhen: • Receiving and then removing pointer hover or keyboard focus triggers additional content to become visible and then hidden, and the visual presentation of the additional content is controlled by the author and not by the user agent.
notes: This applies to content that appears in addition to the triggering of the interactive element itself. Since hidden interactive elements that are made visible on keyboard focus (such as links used to skip to another part of a page/view) do not present additional content, they are not covered by this requirement.

Custom tooltips, sub-menus, and other non-modal popups that display on hover and keyboard focus.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For additional content or focus that appears on hover:

  1. Check that the additional content stays visible and does not automatically close after a time.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Hover Or Focus Content Persistent: Content that appears on pointer hover or keyboard focus remains visible until the hover or keyboard focus trigger is removed, the user dismisses it, or its information is no longer valid.

title: Input Method Flexible
rawBody:
The ability to switch between input methods is available at any time.

:::note
This does not mean that all input technologies (pointer, keyboard, voice, gesture) need to be supported, but if an input modality is supported, it is supported everywhere in the content except where a particular input method is essential to the functionality.
:::

notes: This does not mean that all input technologies (pointer, keyboard, voice, gesture) need to be supported, but if an input modality is supported, it is supported everywhere in the content except where a particular input method is essential to the functionality.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each input:

  1. Set up multiple input types (for example, pointer, keyboard, voice, gesture)
  2. Check that you can switch between inputs and complete functionality.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Input Method Flexible: The ability to switch between input methods is available at any time.

title: Path-based gesture not relied on
rawBody:
Path-based gestures are not the only way of achieving any functionality.

:::except-when
- A path-based gesture is essential to the functionality.
:::

exceptWhen: • A path-based gesture is essential to the functionality.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each path-based gesture:

  1. Check that the functionality is available without a path-based gesture.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Path-based gesture not relied on: Path-based gestures are not the only way of achieving any functionality.

title: Pointer Accessible
rawBody:
Pointer selection of elements moves the keyboard focus to that element, even if the user selects an interactive element and drags away from the element without activation.

:::applies-when
- Content can interfere with pointer or keyboard focus behavior.
:::

:::example
A user scrolls a document down six screens, then clicks on a paragraph with their pointer. The user then presses the <kbd>Tab</kbd> key, which moves the focus to the first interactive component after the position on the screen that was clicked, rather than from the previous position, six screens up the document.
:::

appliesWhen: • Content can interfere with pointer or keyboard focus behavior.
examples: A user scrolls a document down six screens, then clicks on a paragraph with their pointer. The user then presses the Tab key, which moves the focus to the first interactive component after the position on the screen that was clicked, rather than from the previous position, six screens up the document.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For every interactive element that allows pointer selection (including click events on non-interactive elements):

  1. Check that the keyboard focus moves when the pointer selects the element.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Pointer Accessible: Pointer selection of elements moves the keyboard focus to that element, even if the user selects an interactive element and drags away from the element without activation.

title: Bidirectional Navigation
rawBody:
The keyboard interface can always move forward to the next interactive element and back to the previous interactive element.

:::note
Although keyboard navigation is required to be bidirectional, it is not required that it be symmetrical, even though this is usually recommended practice.
:::

:::example
Tabbing through menus, hitting <kbd>space</kbd> to open a menu, tabbing off the end of the menu lands you on the next menu. A <kbd><kbd>shift</kbd>+<kbd>tab</kbd></kbd> may go back to the last item in the previous menu (symmetrical) or to the last menu (not symmetrical but also does not fail this requirement).
:::

notes: Although keyboard navigation is required to be bidirectional, it is not required that it be symmetrical, even though this is usually recommended practice.
examples: Tabbing through menus, hitting space to open a menu, tabbing off the end of the menu lands you on the next menu. A shift+tab may go back to the last item in the previous menu (symmetrical) or to the last menu (not symmetrical but also does not fail this requirement).
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each interactive element:

  1. Check that when tabbing forwards, you can navigate to the interactive element and then to the next interactive element.
  2. Check that when tabbing backwards, you can navigate to the interactive element and then to the previous interactive element.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.
derived.methods: • Use standard HTML to create interactive elements.
derived.recommendedPractices: • Avoid modifying the tab order to be in only one direction.

plainEnglish.summary: Bidirectional Navigation: The keyboard interface can always move forward to the next interactive element and back to the previous interactive element.

title: Custom Keys Documented
rawBody: Documentation for each custom keyboard command is actively available on the page/view to which it applies, or within the applicable process.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each custom keyboard command that works on a page/view:

  1. Check that documentation for the keyboard commands exists.
  2. Check that the documentation is actively available on the page/view to which it applies.
  3. Check that the documentation is actively available within the applicable process.

Expected results

  • #1 is true, and #2 or #3 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Custom Keys Documented: Documentation for each custom keyboard command is actively available on the page/view to which it applies, or within the applicable process.

title: Focus Movement Relevant
rawBody:
Except for skip links and other elements that are hidden but specifically added to aid keyboard navigation, tabbing does not move the keyboard focus onto content that was not visible before the tab action.

:::note
Accordions, dropdown menus, and [ARIA tab panels](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/tabs/) are examples of expandable content. According to this requirement, these would not expand simply because they include an element in the tab-order contained in them. They would either not expand or would not have any tab-order elements in them.
:::

:::example
A menu that expands when you tab to it, but then uses arrow keys to navigate in it would pass. But a menu that expands and then requires you to tab through all the newly-visible elements to navigate past it would fail.
:::

notes: Accordions, dropdown menus, and ARIA tab panels are examples of expandable content. According to this requirement, these would not expand simply because they include an element in the tab-order contained in them. They would either not expand or would not have any tab-order elements in them.
examples: A menu that expands when you tab to it, but then uses arrow keys to navigate in it would pass. But a menu that expands and then requires you to tab through all the newly-visible elements to navigate past it would fail.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For any interactive element:

  1. Check that keyboard focus does not disappear into content that is not visible.
  2. Check that hidden element does not automatically expand (become visible) when the keyboard focus is on it (unless it is a visually hidden element specifically added to aid keyboard navigation) (for example, skip to main content).

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: Focus Movement Relevant: Except for skip links and other elements that are hidden but specifically added to aid keyboard navigation, tabbing does not move the keyboard focus onto content that was not visible before the tab action.

title: Focus Placed
rawBody:
When keyboard focus moves from one context to another within a page/view, whether automatically or by user request, the keyboard focus is preserved so that, when the user returns to the previous context, the keyboard focus is restored to its previous location unless that location no longer exists.

:::example
When a user closes a modal dialog or other popup, keyboard focus is returned to the element that caused the dialog or popup to open.
:::

:::example
When there are tags, with a delete button on each tag, the keyboard focus needs to be moved to a meaningful location after a tag is deleted.
:::

examples: When a user closes a modal dialog or other popup, keyboard focus is returned to the element that caused the dialog or popup to open.
When there are tags, with a delete button on each tag, the keyboard focus needs to be moved to a meaningful location after a tag is deleted.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each situation where elements that have or contain keyboard focus are removed:

  1. Check that the keyboard focus moves to its previous location, or, if that no longer exists, to another meaningful location.

Expected results

  • #1 is true for each situation.
derived.methods: • When removing interactive elements such as filters, dialogs, or popups that currently contain focus, actively place the focus back on the element that led to that element, the previous element within the focus order, or another meaningful location.
derived.recommendedPractices: • Conduct usability testing with screen reader users to evaluate the focus movement.

plainEnglish.summary: Focus Placed: When keyboard focus moves from one context to another within a page/view, whether automatically or by user request, the keyboard focus is preserved so that, when the user returns to the previous context, the keyboard focus is restored to its previous location unless that location no longer exists.

title: Focus user-controlled
rawBody:
The keyboard focus only moves as a result of user interaction.

:::except-when
- The keyboard focus automatically moves to the next interactive elements in keyboard navigation order on completion of some user action, such when the focus moves between the fields for a time-based one-time password (TOTP) code.
- The keyboard focus results from security or emergency situations, such as warning about an imminent session timeout that would cause the user to lose their work.
- The user is informed of the potential keyboard focus move before it happens and given the chance to avoid the move.
:::

exceptWhen:
• The keyboard focus automatically moves to the next interactive elements in keyboard navigation order on completion of some user action, such when the focus moves between the fields for a time-based one-time password (TOTP) code.
  • The keyboard focus results from security or emergency situations, such as warning about an imminent session timeout that would cause the user to lose their work.
  • The user is informed of the potential keyboard focus move before it happens and given the chance to avoid the move.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each time the keyboard focus changes:

  1. Check that one of the following is true:
    • The focus was moved under direct user control
    • A new page / view such as a dialog is introduced and the focus is moved to it
    • The user is informed of the potential move and given the chance to avoid the move
    • The keyboard focus moves to the next item in keyboard navigation order

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Focus user-controlled: The keyboard focus only moves as a result of user interaction.

title: Keyboard Accessible
rawBody:
All content that can be accessed by other input modalities can be accessed using keyboard interface only.

:::note
All content includes content made available via mechanisms including but not limited to hovers, right clicks.
:::

:::note
Other input modalities include pointing devices, voice and speech recognition, gesture, camera, and any other means of input or control.
:::

:::note
The ["Keyboard operable" requirement](#keyboard-operable) allows you to navigate to all actionable elements, but if the next element is 5 screens down, you also need to be able to access all the content. Also, if the content is in expanding sections, you need to not only open them but also access all of the content, not just its actionable elements.
:::

notes: All content includes content made available via mechanisms including but not limited to hovers, right clicks.
Other input modalities include pointing devices, voice and speech recognition, gesture, camera, and any other means of input or control.

The “Keyboard operable” requirement allows you to navigate to all actionable elements, but if the next element is 5 screens down, you also need to be able to access all the content. Also, if the content is in expanding sections, you need to not only open them but also access all of the content, not just its actionable elements.
derived.tests:
Procedure For all content on the page/view:

  1. Check that the content can be viewed using the keyboard and keyboard actions in the Standard Keyboard Navigation & Operation Keys and Techniques;
  2. Check that the content can be viewed using keyboard actions described on the page where it is required or on a page earlier in the process where it is required.

Expected results

  • #1 or #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Keyboard Accessible: All content that can be accessed by other input modalities can be accessed using keyboard interface only.

title: Keyboard Operable
rawBody: All components on the page/view that can be operated by pointer, audio (voice or other), gesture, camera, or other means can be operated using keyboard interface only.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each interactive element:

  1. Check that it can be operated using only the keyboard and keyboard actions in the Standard Keyboard Navigation & Operation Keys and Techniques or described on the page where it is required or on a page earlier in the process where it is required.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Keyboard Operable: All components on the page/view that can be operated by pointer, audio (voice or other), gesture, camera, or other means can be operated using keyboard interface only.

title: No Keyboard Conflicts
rawBody: Custom keyboard commands do not conflict with standard platform keyboard commands or they can be remapped.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each custom keyboard command:

  1. Check that it does not conflict against the standard platform keyboard commands.
  2. Check that it can be remapped.

Expected results

  • #1 or #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: No Keyboard Conflicts: Custom keyboard commands do not conflict with standard platform keyboard commands or they can be remapped.

title: No Keyboard Traps
rawBody:
Components that can be activated or entered using the keyboard interface, can be deactivated or exited using a standard keyboard navigation-operation technique, standard platform keyboard commands.

:::except-when
- The non-standard keyboard navigation technique is described in the page/view or earlier in the process.
:::

:::example
* Ensuring that users can exit a modal dialog, menu, or calendar picker after entering it.
* Ensuring that users can deactivate an animation, video, drop down menu, or carousel after activating it.
:::

exceptWhen: • The non-standard keyboard navigation technique is described in the page/view or earlier in the process.
examples:
• Ensuring that users can exit a modal dialog, menu, or calendar picker after entering it.
  • Ensuring that users can deactivate an animation, video, drop down menu, or carousel after activating it.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each interface element:

  1. Check that you can exit from it in a forward or backward direction.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: No Keyboard Traps: Components that can be activated or entered using the keyboard interface, can be deactivated or exited using a standard keyboard navigation-operation technique, standard platform keyboard commands.

title: Keyboard Effort Comparable
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

- A review has been conducted and changes made (when necessary) to ensure that there is minimal difference between the number of input commands required when using the keyboard interface only and the number of commands when using other input modalities.

:::note
Other input modalities include pointing devices, voice and speech recognition, gesture, camera, and any other means of input or control.
:::

::assertion-required

- title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
- date of when the review was conducted
- date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)
- scope of assertion (if different from the conformance claim)

::assertion-recommended

- copy of the review implementing the use of user interface design principles that include minimizing the difference between the number of input commands required when using the keyboard interface only and the number of commands when using other input modalities
- whether training was provided for authors
- date training was provided
- number or proportion of authors who completed the training
- copy of the user interface design principles document

notes: Other input modalities include pointing devices, voice and speech recognition, gesture, camera, and any other means of input or control.

plainEnglish.summary:
Keyboard Effort Comparable: [Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

- A review has been conducted and changes made (when necessary) to ensure that there is minimal difference between the number of input commands required when using the keyboard interface only and the number of commands when using other input modalities.

title: Navigation Keys Described
rawBody:
If any keyboard action needed to navigate, perceive, and operate the full content of the page/view is not a common keyboard navigation technique, then it is described in the page/view where it is required or on a page/view earlier in the process where it is used. 

:::note
Any platform-related functions are not the responsibility of the author as long as they are not overridden by the content. Examples:

- <kbd>Tab</kbd> and <kbd><kbd>Shift</kbd> + <kbd>Tab</kbd></kbd> to move through elements
- Sticky Keys functionality that allows single key activation of multi-key commands
:::

notes:
Any platform-related functions are not the responsibility of the author as long as they are not overridden by the content. Examples:

  • Tab and Shift + Tab to move through elements
  • Sticky Keys functionality that allows single key activation of multi-key commands
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each keyboard command needed to operate functionality:

  1. Check that it is in the list of common keyboard navigation techniques.
  2. Check that it is described on the page / view where it is required or on a page / view earlier in the process where it is used.

Expected results

  • #1 or #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Navigation Keys Described: If any keyboard action needed to navigate, perceive, and operate the full content of the page/view is not a common keyboard navigation technique, then it is described in the page/view where it is required or on a page/view earlier in the process where it is used.

title: No Repetitive Adjacent Interactive Elements
rawBody:
Adjacent interactive elements that achieve the same outcome are not included in the page/view.

:::except-when
- That outcome is a form of dismissal.
:::

:::note
A common pattern is having a component that includes a linked image and some linked text, where both links go to the same content. Someone using screen reading software can be disoriented from the unnecessary chatter, and a keyboard user has to navigate through more tab stops than should be necessary. Combining adjacent links that go to the same content improves the user experience.
:::

exceptWhen: • That outcome is a form of dismissal.
notes: A common pattern is having a component that includes a linked image and some linked text, where both links go to the same content. Someone using screen reading software can be disoriented from the unnecessary chatter, and a keyboard user has to navigate through more tab stops than should be necessary. Combining adjacent links that go to the same content improves the user experience.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For adjacent interactive elements that achieve the same outcome:

  1. Check that only one of the elements is focusable and available to assistive technology.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.
derived.methods:
• When repetitive interactive elements are used, remove them from the focus and reading order.
  • Use a single link instead of multiple links to the same destination.
derived.recommendedPractices: • Combine repetitive links into a single interactive element.

plainEnglish.summary: No Repetitive Adjacent Interactive Elements: Adjacent interactive elements that achieve the same outcome are not included in the page/view.

title: Consistent Pointer Cancellation
rawBody:
The method of pointer cancellation is consistent for each type of interaction within a set of pages/views.

:::except-when
- It is essential to be different.
:::

:::note
Where it is essential to be different, it can be helpful to alert the user.
:::

exceptWhen: • It is essential to be different.
notes: Where it is essential to be different, it can be helpful to alert the user.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each type of pointer interaction:

  1. Check that it can be canceled with a consistent interaction.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Consistent Pointer Cancellation: The method of pointer cancellation is consistent for each type of interaction within a set of pages/views.

title: Pointer Activation Controllable
rawBody:
At least one of the following is true for functionality that can be activated using a simple pointer input:

No down event
: The down event of the pointer is not used to execute any part of the function.

Cancel or undo
: Completion of the function is on the up event and a mechanism is available to cancel the function before completion, or there is a mechanism to undo the function after completion.

Up reversal
: The up event reverses any outcome of the preceding down event.

:::except-when
- Completing the function on the down event is essential.
:::

:::example
An example of Cancel would be dragging where there is a pickup action on button down, but it can be canceled by dropping anywhere other than the drop area.
:::

:::example
Examples of places where action on down event may be essential include a descending-price auction or a game trigger.
:::

exceptWhen: • Completing the function on the down event is essential.
examples: An example of Cancel would be dragging where there is a pickup action on button down, but it can be canceled by dropping anywhere other than the drop area.
Examples of places where action on down event may be essential include a descending-price auction or a game trigger.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each element that can be activated with a simple pointer:

  1. Check that the down-event of the pointer is not used to execute any part of the function.
  2. Check that completion of the function is on the up-event, and a mechanism is available to abort the function before completion or to undo the function after completion.
  3. Check that the up-event reverses any outcome of the preceding down-event.
  4. Check that completing the function on the down-event is essential.

Expected results

  • Any of #1, #2, #3, or #4 is true.

plainEnglish.summary:
Pointer Activation Controllable: At least one of the following is true for functionality that can be activated using a simple pointer input:

No down event
: The down event of the pointer is not used to execute any part of the function.

title: Pointer Pressure Not Relied On
rawBody:
Specific pointer pressure is not the only way of achieving any functionality.

:::except-when
- Specific pressure is essential to the functionality.
:::

:::example
Specific pressure would be essential to a paintbrush feature or advanced signature verification.
:::

exceptWhen: • Specific pressure is essential to the functionality.
examples: Specific pressure would be essential to a paintbrush feature or advanced signature verification.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each instance of interactive content:

  1. Check that pointer pressure is not the only way to achieve any functionality.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.
derived.methods: • When building in functionality that relies on pointer pressure, add a slider or other control that can complete the same functionality.

plainEnglish.summary: Pointer Pressure Not Relied On: Specific pointer pressure is not the only way of achieving any functionality.

title: Pointer Speed Not Relied On
rawBody:
Functionality does not rely solely on specific pointer speed.

:::except-when
- Specific pointer speed is essential to the functionality.
:::

:::example
Specific pointer speed would be essential to a paintbrush feature, advanced signature verification, or time-constrained gaming.
:::

exceptWhen: • Specific pointer speed is essential to the functionality.
examples: Specific pointer speed would be essential to a paintbrush feature, advanced signature verification, or time-constrained gaming.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each instance of functionality that uses a pointer:

  1. Check that pointer speed is not the only way to achieve any functionality.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Pointer Speed Not Relied On: Functionality does not rely solely on specific pointer speed.

title: Simple Pointer Input Available
rawBody:
All functionality and content available using complex pointer inputs is also available using a simple pointer input, or a sequence of simple pointer inputs that do not require timing.

:::example
Complex pointer inputs include but are not limited to:

- double clicks
- dragging movements
- swipe gestures
- multipoint gestures such as pinching, split tap, or two-finger rotor
- variable pressure or timing
:::

:::note
Complex pointer inputs are not banned, but they cannot be the only way to accomplish an action.
:::

:::note
Simple pointer input is different than single pointer input and is more restrictive than simply using a single pointer.
:::

notes: Complex pointer inputs are not banned, but they cannot be the only way to accomplish an action.
Simple pointer input is different than single pointer input and is more restrictive than simply using a single pointer.
examples:
Complex pointer inputs include but are not limited to:

  • double clicks
  • dragging movements
  • swipe gestures
  • multipoint gestures such as pinching, split tap, or two-finger rotor
  • variable pressure or timing
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each functionality that uses pointer input other than simple pointer input:

  1. Check that it can also be operated by a simple pointer input or a sequence of simple pointer inputs that do not require timing.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Simple Pointer Input Available: All functionality and content available using complex pointer inputs is also available using a simple pointer input, or a sequence of simple pointer inputs that do not require timing.

title: Generated Speech Testing
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

- We have tested voice input and communication systems with generated speech to ensure the systems work with artificial speech as well as human speech.

::assertion-required

- title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
