- date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)

::assertion-recommended

- systems tested
- accuracy rates

plainEnglish.summary:
Generated Speech Testing: [Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

- We have tested voice input and communication systems with generated speech to ensure the systems work with artificial speech as well as human speech.

title: Real-time text available
rawBody: A real-time text option is available for real-time bidirectional voice communication.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each place where speech is used for communication (with human or AI):

  1. Check that there is an alternative way to achieve the same function using real-time text.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.
derived.methods: • Provide a chat option for any voice communication.

plainEnglish.summary: Real-time text available: A real-time text option is available for real-time bidirectional voice communication.

title: Speech Not Relied On
rawBody:
Content or functionality does not rely on speech alone.

:::except-when
- Speech input is essential to the functionality.
:::

exceptWhen: • Speech input is essential to the functionality.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each functionality or content that is accessed using speech input:

  1. Check that there is another way to complete the functionality.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.
derived.methods: • When speech input is supported, an additional way of providing input is also supported.

plainEnglish.summary: Speech Not Relied On: Content or functionality does not rely on speech alone.

title: Changes To Elements Notified
rawBody: Changes to interactive element names, roles, values, or states are visually and programmatically indicated.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each interactive element:

  1. Confirm that the role, value, and state (when applicable) are visually indicated in all states.
  2. Inspect the code and accessibility tree (when available) to confirm that the name, role, value and state (when applicable) are indicated.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.
derived.methods:
• Add code that clearly defines the name, role, value and state.
  • Visually indicate the names, roles, and values of the interactive element.
  • HTML: HTML tags or ARIA

plainEnglish.summary: Changes To Elements Notified: Changes to interactive element names, roles, values, or states are visually and programmatically indicated.

title: Input Constraints Used
rawBody:
Field constraints and conditions are available.

:::example
* required line length
* date format
* password format
:::

examples:
• required line length
  • date format
  • password format
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each input:

  1. Confirm it has a visual information that describes the constraint.
  2. Inspect the code and accessibility tree (when applicable) and confirm that the constraint is programmatically listed in the code and associated with the input.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.
derived.methods: • HTML: To programmatically indicate, use the pattern attribute or write the information in a label; to visually indicate, add the requirements to the page near the input.

plainEnglish.summary: Input Constraints Used: Field constraints and conditions are available.

title: Interactive Element Contrast Sufficient
rawBody:
Visual information required to identify interactive elements and states meet a minimum contrast ratio test.

:::except-when
* The interactive element is inactive, or
* The appearance of the component is determined by the user agent and not modified by the content author.
:::

exceptWhen:
• The interactive element is inactive, or
  • The appearance of the component is determined by the user agent and not modified by the content author.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each interactive element:

  1. Identify which visual information defines the boundaries of the interactive area.
  2. Check if the visual information meets the minimum contrast ratio test.
  3. For each possible state, repeat step 1 and 2.

Expected results

  • #2 is true for each state.

plainEnglish.summary: Interactive Element Contrast Sufficient: Visual information required to identify interactive elements and states meet a minimum contrast ratio test.

title: Interactive Element Importance Indicated
rawBody: The importance of interactive components is indicated.

plainEnglish.summary: Interactive Element Importance Indicated: The importance of interactive components is indicated.

title: Interactive Element Names Available
rawBody:
Persistent names (including labels) that identify the purpose of the interactive element are visually and programmatically available. 

:::note
Visible labels can be text or non-text, for instance icons.
:::

notes: Visible labels can be text or non-text, for instance icons.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each interactive element:

  1. Confirm it has a visual label that describes the element.
  2. Confirm the visual label persists during use.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.
derived.methods: • Provide unique, descriptive text or image (icon) for each interactive element.
derived.recommendedPractices:
• To ensure clarity, pair an icon with a persistent visible text label, or only use a persistent visible text label.
  • When an icon is the only visual label, provide a tooltip (hover label) with the text description.

plainEnglish.summary: Every clickable or interactive element (buttons, links, form fields, tabs) must have a persistent visual and programmatic name so users know what it does.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Users rely on labels to know what will happen when they click or tap. Screen readers need programmatic names to announce controls accurately.
plainEnglish.realWorldExample: An icon-only magnifying glass button must have a persistent name like 'Search' via `aria-label` or visible text plus tooltip.

personaBreakdown.designer: Pair icon-only buttons with persistent text labels or visible tooltips.
personaBreakdown.developer: Provide unique text or `aria-label` for every interactive control.
personaBreakdown.qa: Verify that screen readers announce a meaningful name for every button and link.
personaBreakdown.productManager: Ensure design assets include accessible names for icon controls.

statusSummary.workingGroupDebate: W3C consensus is strong on requiring persistent names; discussions focus on icon-only controls and dynamic aria-labels.
statusSummary.keyChallenges: Ensuring icon-only interfaces remain accessible without cluttering visual layouts.

testingGuide.manualKeyboard: Tab to control, verify outline and visual label.
testingGuide.screenReader: Screen reader speaks label upon focus.

wcag22Comparison.deltaExplanation: WCAG 3 unifies visual and programmatic naming rules and strongly recommends persistent visible text pairing over aria-label alone.

title: Interactive Elements Distinguishable
rawBody: Interactive elements are visually distinguishable without interaction from static content and include visual cues on how to use them.

derived.methods: • Add visual indicators, such as shading, border, drop-down arrow, or placement, to interactive elements.
derived.recommendedPractices: • Document interactive indicators and designs in a style guide.

plainEnglish.summary: Interactive Elements Distinguishable: Interactive elements are visually distinguishable without interaction from static content and include visual cues on how to use them.

title: Label Included In Programmatic Name
rawBody: The programmatic name includes the visual label.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each interactive element:

  1. Identify the interactive elements’ programmatic name.
  2. Identify the interactive element’s visual name.
  3. Check that #1 includes all of #2.

Expected results

  • #3 is true.
derived.methods: • Code the same name as you display.
derived.recommendedPractices: • Use unique names and keep the programmatic and visual names the same.

plainEnglish.summary: Label Included In Programmatic Name: The programmatic name includes the visual label.

title: Roles, values, states, properties available
rawBody: Accurate names, roles, values, and states are available for interactive elements.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each interactive element:

  1. Inspect the code and accessibility tree (when available) to confirm that the role, value, state, and properties (when applicable) are indicated.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.
derived.methods:
• HTML: Use HTML elements according to specification.
  • ARIA: Add roles, values, states, and properties according to specification.

plainEnglish.summary: Roles, values, states, properties available: Accurate names, roles, values, and states are available for interactive elements.

title: Consistent Control Location
rawBody:
Where an interactive element with the same purpose is used across pages/views, its visual position in the layout is maintained.

:::except-when
- The location changes due to a page variation or viewport change, or
- The layout changes due to being part of a process.
:::

:::example
An e-commerce checkout is an example of where the layout might change within a longer process.
:::

exceptWhen:
• The location changes due to a page variation or viewport change, or
  • The layout changes due to being part of a process.
examples: An e-commerce checkout is an example of where the layout might change within a longer process.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each interactive component in a set of pages/views:

  1. Check that components appear in the same relative visual position across pages/views, except when exceptions apply.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.
derived.methods:
• Establish a design system with documented rules for consistent placement of common interactive components (for example, navigation menus, search bars, and action buttons).
  • Reuse the same components across pages/views instead of recreating them.
derived.recommendedPractices: • If a visual position must change, document why and consider providing cues (for example, animations and labels) to reduce confusion.

plainEnglish.summary: Consistent Control Location: Where an interactive element with the same purpose is used across pages/views, its visual position in the layout is maintained.

title: Consistent Interactions
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

- A review has been conducted and changes made (when necessary) to ensure that Components with the same functionality behave consistently:
  - Components that perform the same function behave in the same way and use the same visual indicators.
  - Within the component, interactive elements with the same function have consistent labels.
  - Standard user interface designs for the platform are used when applicable.

::assertion-required

- title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
- date of when the review was completed
- date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)

::assertion-recommended

- results from the review
- process or policy for maintaining the review

plainEnglish.summary:
Consistent Interactions: [Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

- A review has been conducted and changes made (when necessary) to ensure that Components with the same functionality behave consistently:
  - Components that perform the same function behave in the same way and use the same visual indicators.

title: Conventional Pattern Used
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

- A review has been conducted and changes made (when necessary) to ensure that Components follow established conventions:
  - Each component follows applicable platform conventions for how users interact with that type of component.
  - If a component library is used, then each component in the library: 
    - is tested for accessibility before being used
    - follows applicable platform conventions for how users interact with that type of component

::assertion-required

- title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
- date of when the review was completed
- date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)

::assertion-recommended

- results from the review
- process or policy for maintaining the review

:::note
A component library specifies a set of standardized components used in a product or products. It can include code to use, but at a minimum would define how the component is used and define pointer, keyboard, and assistive technology interactions.

Using a component library can help larger teams and organizations provide a consistent experience. 

Examples of component libraries include [GDS](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/), [Carbon Design System](https://www.carbondesignsystem.com/), and [Lion](https://lion.js.org/).

Examples of platform patterns are [ARIA Platform Authoring Guide](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/) (web), [Apple human interface guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/components), and [Android Material Design](https://m2.material.io/components?platform=android).
:::

Conventional Pattern Used: [Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

- A review has been conducted and changes made (when necessary) to ensure that Components follow established conventions:
  - Each component follows applicable platform conventions for how users interact with that type of component.

title: Default Focus Indicator Used
rawBody: The focusable item uses the user agent default focus indicator.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For user agents that allow the customization of focus indicators:

  1. Use the keyboard to move focus onto the item.
  2. Check that the focus indicator is the user agent’s default indicator.
  3. For platform display changes, check that the focus indicator’s color is correct for the type of element.

Expected results

  • #2 and #3 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: Default Focus Indicator Used: The focusable item uses the user agent default focus indicator.

title: Focus Indicator Contrast Sufficient
rawBody:
If a custom focus indicator is used, it has sufficient adjacent contrast and change of contrast.

:::applies-when
* the user agent's default focus indicator is replaced by a custom focus indicator.
:::

appliesWhen: • the user agent’s default focus indicator is replaced by a custom focus indicator.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each element able to attain focus:

  1. Using a keyboard, tab to the component.
  2. Check that the focus indicator contrast meets the minimum contrast ratio test.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Focus Indicator Contrast Sufficient: If a custom focus indicator is used, it has sufficient adjacent contrast and change of contrast.

title: Focus Indicator Size Sufficient
rawBody:
If a custom focus indicator is used, it has sufficient size and adjacency.

:::applies-when
* the user agent's default focus indicator is replaced by a custom focus indicator.
:::

appliesWhen: • the user agent’s default focus indicator is replaced by a custom focus indicator.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each custom focus indicator:

  1. Check that the focus indicator is at least as large as the area of a 2 CSS pixel thick perimeter of the unfocused component or sub-component, and
  2. Check that the focus indicator has a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 between the same pixels in the focused and unfocused states.

Except when

  • the focus indicator is determined by the user agent and cannot be adjusted by the author, or the focus indicator and the indicator’s background color are not modified by the author.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: Focus Indicator Size Sufficient: If a custom focus indicator is used, it has sufficient size and adjacency.

title: Focus Indicator Style Guide
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

- Our organization has a style guide that includes guidance on focus indicators and a policy and/or processes that the style guide must be followed.

::assertion-required

- title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)

- whether training was provided for authors
    - date training was provided
    - number or proportion of authors who completed the training
- copy of the design style guide (if any) where focus style has been defined

plainEnglish.summary:
Focus Indicator Style Guide: [Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

- Our organization has a style guide that includes guidance on focus indicators and a policy and/or processes that the style guide must be followed.

title: Focus Order Meaningful
rawBody:
The keyboard focus moves sequentially through content in an order and way that preserves meaning and operability.

:::note
- The Common Keyboard Navigation Techniques are considered logical by default.
- Having the navigation follow a consistent pattern on the page would be an indication of logic (if it is not consistently random).
- A strictly start-to-end order is not required.
- Linear means in a single direction (forward/backward) - and is not required as long the non-linear (x-y) technique is in the Common Keyboard Navigation Techniques or is described on the page or where the user will encounter it prior.
:::

notes:
• The Common Keyboard Navigation Techniques are considered logical by default.
  • Having the navigation follow a consistent pattern on the page would be an indication of logic (if it is not consistently random).
  • A strictly start-to-end order is not required.
  • Linear means in a single direction (forward/backward) - and is not required as long the non-linear (x-y) technique is in the Common Keyboard Navigation Techniques or is described on the page or where the user will encounter it prior.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each page/view:

  1. Determine the logical order of the interactive elements.
  2. Starting with the first focusable element in the page/view, tab through the interactive elements in the content.
  3. Check that the focus order of the interactive elements in the content is the same as the logical order in #1.

Expected results

  • #3 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Focus Order Meaningful: The keyboard focus moves sequentially through content in an order and way that preserves meaning and operability.

title: Focus Relevant
rawBody: The focus order does not include hidden, static, or groups of repeated interactive elements.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For groups of repeated interactive elements (for example, a site-wide navigation bar on a website):

  1. Check that a method of skipping them is available.
  2. Check that hidden interactive elements do not receive focus.
  3. Check that static elements do not receive focus.

Expected results

  • #1, #2, and #3 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: Focus Relevant: The focus order does not include hidden, static, or groups of repeated interactive elements.

title: Focus Retained
rawBody: A user can focus on a content "area", such as a modal or popup, then resume their view of all content using a limited number of steps.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each situation where the keyboard focus is removed:

  1. Check that the keyboard focus moves to its previous location, or, if that no longer exists, to another meaningful location.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Focus Retained: A user can focus on a content "area", such as a modal or popup, then resume their view of all content using a limited number of steps.

title: Default Pointer Used
rawBody:
The user can ensure that the appearance of the pointer is not overridden by the authored interface.

:::except-when
- Changing the pointer appearance is essential.
:::

exceptWhen: • Changing the pointer appearance is essential.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each pointer indicator:

  1. Check that the pointer uses the standard platform indicator.
  2. Check for a setting that the user can enable to use the standard platform indicator.

Expected results

  • #1 or #2 is true.
derived.methods:
• No scripting or styling overrides the pointer indicator appearance.
  • Provide a setting that removes any overrides to the pointer indicator appearance.

plainEnglish.summary: Default Pointer Used: The user can ensure that the appearance of the pointer is not overridden by the authored interface.

title: Enhanced Pointer Available
rawBody: Provide a more visible pointer indicator than the platform default. The enhanced pointer indicator can be enabled in a setting, and be visible temporarily (for a few seconds) or permanently.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each pointer indicator:

  1. Check for a setting that increases the visibility.
  2. Check that it works in the conformance scope of web pages/views.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.
derived.methods: • Provide a setting to adjust the pointer indicator.

plainEnglish.summary: Enhanced Pointer Available: Provide a more visible pointer indicator than the platform default.

title: Pointer activation indicated (enhanced)
rawBody:
The user can choose to always have a visible pointer indicator.

:::applies-when
- The platform does not use a visible pointer indicator.
:::

:::note
This is primarily aimed at eye-tracking and touch-screens, where it is useful for the user to be able to have a visible indicator, but it wouldn't be universal. This aims to avoid it being in the way for some users.
:::

appliesWhen: • The platform does not use a visible pointer indicator.
notes: This is primarily aimed at eye-tracking and touch-screens, where it is useful for the user to be able to have a visible indicator, but it wouldn’t be universal. This aims to avoid it being in the way for some users.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each pointer indicator:

  1. Check the settings of the platform or conformance scope for the ability to have an always-visible pointer indicator.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Pointer activation indicated (enhanced): The user can choose to always have a visible pointer indicator.

title: Pointer activation indicated (minimum)
rawBody:
There is a visible indication of the activation of an interactive element when selected by the pointer.

:::applies-when
- The platform does not use a visible pointer indicator.
:::

:::note
This is primarily aimed at touch-interfaces and VR where you don’t have a pointer indicator, but do need to know when something has been selected.
:::

appliesWhen: • The platform does not use a visible pointer indicator.
notes: This is primarily aimed at touch-interfaces and VR where you don’t have a pointer indicator, but do need to know when something has been selected.
derived.tests:
Procedure

Where the platform does not use a visible pointer indicator, for each interactive element:

  1. Check that there is an indicator of activation.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Pointer activation indicated (minimum): There is a visible indication of the activation of an interactive element when selected by the pointer.

title: Pointer Contrast Sufficient
rawBody:
The default pointer meets the @@[non-text-contrast] requirement, and is at least as large as the platform default.

:::applies-when
* the pointer indicator appearance can be adjusted from the platform default.
:::

:::note
There can be multiple types of pointer indicator. For example, arrow, hand, caret. The size requirement applies to whichever type of indicator would be the default for that scenario.
:::

appliesWhen: • the pointer indicator appearance can be adjusted from the platform default.
notes: There can be multiple types of pointer indicator. For example, arrow, hand, caret. The size requirement applies to whichever type of indicator would be the default for that scenario.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each custom pointer indicator:

  1. Identify which visual information defines the boundaries of the interactive area.
  2. Check if the visual information meets the minimum contrast ratio test.
  3. For each possible state, repeat step 1 and 2.

Expected results

  • #2 is true for each state.

plainEnglish.summary: Pointer Contrast Sufficient: The default pointer meets the @@[non-text-contrast] requirement, and is at least as large as the platform default.

title: Pointer Focus Indicated
rawBody:
There is a visible pointer indicator.

:::except-when
- The pointer is on a video - it can be hidden if there is a pointer mechanism to un-hide the pointer indicator.
- The pointer controls the direction of view in a virtual or real world environment.
:::

:::note
Examples of pointers which do not always show the pointer indicator:

- A touch-screen interface does not need to have an indicator as the pointer is not on an element before activating it.
- An eye-tracking interface highlights the element under the gaze of the user, but otherwise does not have a pointer indicator. 
- A game where you use the pointer to move the entire view around a virtual environment.
:::

exceptWhen:
• The pointer is on a video - it can be hidden if there is a pointer mechanism to un-hide the pointer indicator.
  • The pointer controls the direction of view in a virtual or real world environment.
notes:
Examples of pointers which do not always show the pointer indicator:

  • A touch-screen interface does not need to have an indicator as the pointer is not on an element before activating it.
  • An eye-tracking interface highlights the element under the gaze of the user, but otherwise does not have a pointer indicator.
  • A game where you use the pointer to move the entire view around a virtual environment.
derived.tests:
Procedure

With appropriate user settings enabled:

  1. Move the pointer (mouse, eye tracker, hand gesture in VR space, …).
  2. Check that there is some form of indication of where the user is pointing to.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.
derived.methods: • Interactive elements are highlighted when the pointer is on the element. For example, a set of image links are shown, and the one under the pointer is highlighted with an outline or change in size.

plainEnglish.summary: Pointer Focus Indicated: There is a visible pointer indicator.

title: Pointer Visible
rawBody:
The pointer indicator is always visible.

:::except-when
- The pointer is on a video and is not moving.
- The pointer controls the direction of view in a virtual or real world environment.
:::

exceptWhen:
• The pointer is on a video and is not moving.
  • The pointer controls the direction of view in a virtual or real world environment.
derived.tests:
Procedure

If the pointer is ever not visible:

  1. Check that it meets one of the exceptions.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.
derived.methods: • No styling or scripting hides the pointer indicator.

plainEnglish.summary: Pointer Visible: The pointer indicator is always visible.

title: Infinite Scrolling Controllable
rawBody: Where content includes infinite scrolling, a mechanism is provided prior to the scrolling content that allows users to switch off infinite scrolling. No content should be rendered unavailable as a result of switching on this option.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each instance of infinite scrolling:

  1. Check that the preceding content includes a mechanism to allow infinite scrolling to be switched off.
  2. Check that all content that was available via infinite scrolling is also available without relying on it.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: Infinite Scrolling Controllable: Where content includes infinite scrolling, a mechanism is provided prior to the scrolling content that allows users to switch off infinite scrolling.

title: Overlay Content Dismissible
rawBody: When new content becomes visible and covers the main content, a mechanism is available to dismiss the new content.

derived.tests:
Modal dialogs on interaction

Procedure

For each element that opens a modal dialog when interacted with:

  1. Open the dialog.
  2. Check that the dialog includes a mechanism to allow the dialog to be dismissed.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.
derived.methods:
• The ‘Escape’ (Esc) key closes new content.
  • An accessible ‘close’ button is provided to close the new content.

plainEnglish.summary: Overlay Content Dismissible: When new content becomes visible and covers the main content, a mechanism is available to dismiss the new content.

title: Conventional Layout Review
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

* We have reviewed layout conventions for similar products or processes.
* The layout used follows a conventional pattern or a tested non-conventional pattern was used.

::assertion-required

* title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
* date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)

::assertion-recommended

* report covering review of layouts for similar products or processes
* design log capturing decision to use specific layouts
* if a non-conventional layout is used, usability testing results that demonstrate the utility of the approach taken

plainEnglish.summary:
Conventional Layout Review: [Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

 We have reviewed layout conventions for similar products or processes.

title: Blocks of content available (enhanced)
rawBody: Styling is used to enhance the visual separation between meaningful blocks of content.

derived.tests:
Visually identifiable meaningful blocks of content

Procedure

For each meaningful block of content in the page/view:

  1. Check that each meaningful block of content is grouped by one or more of the following characteristics:
    • Color or lightness — the same color scheme is used (Note that this should also meet requirements for ‘Color alone’ and ‘Contrast’)
    • Borders — blocks are contained within the same borders
    • Spacing — blocks are grouped based on their proximity to others within the same area, while spacing is used to separate different sections of content
    • Font — blocks are presented with similar font families
    • Position — blocks are located in the same area of the page/view (for example, header, navigation, footer)
    • Repeated visual feature — blocks contain a consistent visual feature (for example, bullets in a list, checkbox)

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Blocks of content available (enhanced): Styling is used to enhance the visual separation between meaningful blocks of content.

title: Blocks of content available (minimum)
rawBody: Meaningful blocks of content are programmatically determinable and visually presented with sufficient surrounding space.

derived.tests:
HTML sufficient space

Procedure

  1. Identify meaningful blocks of content in the page/view that are not bounded by a visual border.
  2. Examine the computed style to determine the total of margin, padding and border spacing.
  3. Check that the spacing between all adjacent meaningful blocks of content is sufficient.

Expected results

  • #3 is true.

Programmatically identifiable meaningful blocks of content

Procedure

For each meaningful blocks of content in the page/view:

  1. Check that an appropriate role is being used for the meaningful blocks of content in the source code.
  2. Check using assistive technology that an appropriate role is being used for the meaningful blocks of content.

Expected results

  • #1 or #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Blocks of content available (minimum): Meaningful blocks of content are programmatically determinable and visually presented with sufficient surrounding space.

title: Clear Structure Review
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

plainEnglish.summary: Required Action Available: The interface indicates when user input or action is required in order to proceed to the next step.

title: Going Back Supported
rawBody:
In a multi-step process, the interface supports stepping backwards in a process and returning to the current point without data loss.

:::except-when
- It is essential that the user cannot step back in a process.
:::
 
:::example
Certain tests in education may require that the student cannot go back through previously-submitted responses and change them.
:::

exceptWhen: • It is essential that the user cannot step back in a process.
examples: Certain tests in education may require that the student cannot go back through previously-submitted responses and change them.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For multi-step processes:

  1. Check that the user is prompted to review and confirm data.
  2. Check that the user is allowed to return to previous steps to review and change the data.
  3. Check that if a summary of all data input by the user is provided before the transaction is committed, and that a method is provided to correct errors, if necessary.

Expected results

  • #1, #2, or #3 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Going Back Supported: In a multi-step process, the interface supports stepping backwards in a process and returning to the current point without data loss.

title: No Redundant Entry
rawBody:
Information previously entered by or provided to the user that is required to be entered again in the same process is either auto-populated, or available for the user to select.

:::except-when
- Re-entering the information is essential,
- The information is required to ensure the security of the content, or
- Previously entered information is no longer valid.
:::

exceptWhen:
• Re-entering the information is essential,
  • The information is required to ensure the security of the content, or
  • Previously entered information is no longer valid.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For any process that requires the user to enter information:

  1. Check whether the information has already been requested in a previous step of the process.
  2. Check that the information entered previously is prepopulated in the respective field(s) or is displayed on the page for copying.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: No Redundant Entry: Information previously entered by or provided to the user that is required to be entered again in the same process is either auto-populated, or available for the user to select.

title: Progress Saved
rawBody:
Data entry and other task completion processes allow saving and resuming from the current step in the task.

:::except-when
- The task completion is part of a real-time event, and no alternative to the time limit is possible.
:::

:::example
Real-time events would include but are not limited to auctions or ticket sales.
:::

exceptWhen: • The task completion is part of a real-time event, and no alternative to the time limit is possible.
examples: Real-time events would include but are not limited to auctions or ticket sales.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For any processes that require the user to enter information:

  1. Log in, if needed, and begin the timed activity.
  2. Allow the session to time out.
  3. Submit or save the data.
  4. Log out if logged in.
  5. Re-authenticate and log back in.
  6. Check that the process can continue from where you left off and be completed without loss of data, including the original data and any changes made after re-authentication.
  7. Check that the process used to save the information submitted in step 3 is not stored on the server. (Note: This requires knowledge of the technology and features used to implement the technique.)

Expected results

  • #6 and #7 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: Progress Saved: Data entry and other task completion processes allow saving and resuming from the current step in the task.

title: Usability Testing For Unnecessary Steps
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

* Usability testing has been conducted to review for unnecessary steps in the process or unnecessary information being requested.
* The sample of test participants included people with cognitive disabilities and/or mental health based disabilities.

::assertion-required

* title, role, or organization making the assertion
* date of assertion

::assertion-recommended

* maintained records of usability testing protocol, scope of the testing, and results
* number of participants and disabilities represented within the group of participants
* record of actions taken to address identified issues

plainEnglish.summary:
Usability Testing For Unnecessary Steps: [Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

 Usability testing has been conducted to review for unnecessary steps in the process or unnecessary information being requested.

title: Abbreviations Explained
rawBody:
Explanations of abbreviations are available when first used. 

:::except-when
- the abbreviation is:
    * used so often it has become a word with its own dictionary entry, such as "scuba," "info," and "HTML",
    * used in a logo, or
    * included in a longer phrase, such as "brand DNA," whose meaning needs to be defined to meet the [non-literal language requirement](#non-literal-language-explained).
:::

:::example
Abbreviation is introduced after first expanded use of the term.

> "He has Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (ARFID)."

Abbreviation is linked to a glossary entry or tooltip.

> "He has [ARFID]."
:::

exceptWhen:
• the abbreviation is:
    • used so often it has become a word with its own dictionary entry, such as “scuba,” “info,” and “HTML”,
    • used in a logo, or
    • included in a longer phrase, such as “brand DNA,” whose meaning needs to be defined to meet the non-literal language requirement.
examples:
Abbreviation is introduced after first expanded use of the term.

“He has Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (ARFID).”

Abbreviation is linked to a glossary entry or tooltip.

“He has [ARFID].”
derived.tests:
Procedure

For any abbreviation in the content:

  1. Check that an explanation is available for the first use of the abbreviation.
  2. For an abbreviation that has no explanation available, check that it is included in a dictionary intended for the general public.

Expected result

  • #1 or #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Abbreviations Explained: Explanations of abbreviations are available when first used.

title: Clear Language Review
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

* Our organization has a process and policy to review text content for clear language before publication. The process includes confirming:
  * All of the core requirements in the ‘Clear Language’ guideline are met.
  * Verb tense is chosen for ease of understanding.
  * Content uses short paragraphs.
  * Paragraphs that convey information begin with a sentence stating the main point or purpose (often called a topic sentence).
  * If a style guide is used by content authors, it must provide guidance on these aspects of clear language. 
  * If author training is provided, it must provide guidance on these aspects of clear language.

::assertion-required

* title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
* date of when the policy was implemented
* date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)

::assertion-recommended

* copy of the policy implementing the clear language review
* date author training was provided (if any)
* number or proportion of authors who completed the training
* copy of the style guide (if any) where clear language review has been defined

plainEnglish.summary:
Clear Language Review: [Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

 Our organization has a process and policy to review text content for clear language before publication.

title: Common Words Used
rawBody: Common words are used, and definitions are available for uncommon words. :::applies-when * human languages have more than 1,500 words. ::: :::except-when * the words are for names of people or places, or * the language does not have a high-frequency corpus. ::: :::note This is not a core requirement because a list of common words would not cover terms that are known by specific audiences, such as accounting terms on an accounting site. However, in future guidance for policymakers, it is an example of a supplemental requirement that could be made mandatory for public service and education providers. Lists of common words are called high-frequency corpora. They exist for many languages including Arabic, Hindi, Mandarin, and Russian as well as American English, British English, and Canadian English. ::: :::ednote Research shows that using common words and defining uncommon words improves understanding. Making Content Usable for People with Cognitive and Learning Disabilities recommends using the 1,500 highest-frequency words or phrases because people with severe language impairments are most likely to know these terms. However, more research is needed to confirm if the same threshold applies to many languages for distinguishing common from uncommon words. :::

appliesWhen: • human languages have more than 1,500 words.
exceptWhen:
• the words are for names of people or places, or
  • the language does not have a high-frequency corpus.
notes:
This is not a core requirement because a list of common words would not cover terms that are known by specific audiences, such as accounting terms on an accounting site. However, in future guidance for policymakers, it is an example of a supplemental requirement that could be made mandatory for public service and education providers.

Lists of common words are called high-frequency corpora. They exist for many languages including Arabic, Hindi, Mandarin, and Russian as well as American English, British English, and Canadian English.
editorNotes: Research shows that using common words and defining uncommon words improves understanding. Making Content Usable for People with Cognitive and Learning Disabilities recommends using the 1,500 highest-frequency words or phrases because people with severe language impairments are most likely to know these terms. However, more research is needed to confirm if the same threshold applies to many languages for distinguishing common from uncommon words.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each word:

  1. Check that the word appears in the 1,500 most common words in a high-frequency corpus for the language used.
  2. If the word is not in the list of the 1,500 most common words, check that it has a definition available within the page/view.
  3. Check that a technology in the accessibility support set meets ‘Common words used.’

Expected results

  • #1, #2, or #3 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Common Words Used: Common words are used, and definitions are available for uncommon words.

title: Diacritics Available
rawBody: Diacritics required to identify the correct meaning of each word are available. :::applies-when * a human language has a version that removes diacritics for proficient readers. ::: :::note A diacritic is a small mark that is added to a letter or character that changes how it is pronounced or what it means. Diacritics may appear above, below, within, or between letters or characters. ::: :::note Hebrew and Arabic are examples of human languages that omit diacritics for proficient readers. ::: :::example The Hebrew word אמר, with three consonants and no diacritics * Without diacritics to represent the vowels, אמר can represent different verb and noun forms of “to say.” * Readers must rely on context to determine the intended pronunciation and meaning. ::: :::example The Hebrew word אָמַר, with diacritics under two of the three consonants * A diacritic (whose unicode looks similar to an uppercase T) under the א makes an “ah” sound. * A horizontal mark under the מ makes a short “a” sound. * Pronunciation: ah-mar * Meaning: "He said" ::: :::example The Hebrew word יֹאמַר, with diacritics in front of the first consonant and under another * A mark (that looks similar to a floating comma) in front of the word indicates future tense, masculine. * A dot above the prefix makes an "o" sound. * A horizontal mark under the מ makes a short “a” sound. * Pronunciation: yo-mar * Meaning: "He will say" ::: :::example The Hebrew word אֹמֶר, with a different set of diacritics above one consonant and under another * A dot above the first letter makes an “o” sound. * Three dots forming a small triangle under the מ make a short “e” sound. * Pronunciation: oh-mer * Meaning: "utterance; saying" (noun) :::

appliesWhen: • a human language has a version that removes diacritics for proficient readers.
notes: A diacritic is a small mark that is added to a letter or character that changes how it is pronounced or what it means. Diacritics may appear above, below, within, or between letters or characters.
Hebrew and Arabic are examples of human languages that omit diacritics for proficient readers.
examples:
The Hebrew word אמר, with three consonants and no diacritics

  • Without diacritics to represent the vowels, אמר can represent different verb and noun forms of “to say.”
  • Readers must rely on context to determine the intended pronunciation and meaning.

The Hebrew word אָמַר, with diacritics under two of the three consonants

  • A diacritic (whose unicode looks similar to an uppercase T) under the א makes an “ah” sound.
  • A horizontal mark under the מ makes a short “a” sound.
  • Pronunciation: ah-mar
  • Meaning: “He said”

The Hebrew word יֹאמַר, with diacritics in front of the first consonant and under another

  • A mark (that looks similar to a floating comma) in front of the word indicates future tense, masculine.
  • A dot above the prefix makes an “o” sound.
  • A horizontal mark under the מ makes a short “a” sound.
  • Pronunciation: yo-mar
  • Meaning: “He will say”

The Hebrew word אֹמֶר, with a different set of diacritics above one consonant and under another

  • A dot above the first letter makes an “o” sound.
  • Three dots forming a small triangle under the מ make a short “e” sound.
  • Pronunciation: oh-mer
  • Meaning: “utterance; saying” (noun)
derived.tests:
Procedure

For all text content:

  1. Check for content that has missing diacritics.
  2. Check that an alternative version to text identified in #1 is provided that includes diacritics needed to identify the correct meaning of each word.
  3. Check that the accessibility support set meets ‘Diacritics available’.

Expected results

  • #2 or #3 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Diacritics Available: Diacritics required to identify the correct meaning of each word are available.

title: No Nested Clauses
rawBody:
Sentences do not include nested clauses.

:::except-when
- text content:
    * is poetic, scriptural, artistic, or expressive rather than informational, or
    * provides legal information.
:::

:::example
The sentence:

> "The teacher was surprised that the student who did well on yesterday's test was absent today."

Includes the nested clause "who did well on yesterday's test" of the clause "was surprised that the student ... was absent today".

This could be written without the nested clause as:

> "The teacher was surprised that the student was absent today. This was unexpected because he did well on yesterday's test."
:::

exceptWhen:
• text content:
    • is poetic, scriptural, artistic, or expressive rather than informational, or
    • provides legal information.
examples:
The sentence:

“The teacher was surprised that the student who did well on yesterday’s test was absent today.”

Includes the nested clause “who did well on yesterday’s test” of the clause “was surprised that the student … was absent today”.

This could be written without the nested clause as:

“The teacher was surprised that the student was absent today. This was unexpected because he did well on yesterday’s test.”
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each sentence: For all nested clauses in the sentence (introduced by nesting conjunctions such as ‘because’, ‘although’, ‘if’, ‘that’, ‘which’, ‘who’, ‘when’, and ‘where’).

  1. Check that each initial nested clause does not contain other nested clauses within it.
  2. Check that a technology in the accessibility support set meets ‘No nested clauses’.

Expected results

  • #1 or #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: No Nested Clauses: Sentences do not include nested clauses.

title: No Unnecessary Words
rawBody:
Sentences do not include unnecessary words.

:::except-when
- text content is:
  * poetic,
  * scriptural,
  * artistic, or
  * expressive rather than informational.
:::

:::example
* redundant modifiers such as ‘free gift’ and ‘past history’ 
* double negatives to express a positive such as ‘She didn't see nothing’ (which can be shortened to ‘She saw nothing’)
* indirect phrasing such as ‘at this point in time’ (which can be shortened to ‘now’)
* noun versions of verbs, such as ‘take into consideration’ (which can be shortened to ‘consider’)
:::

:::note 
Automated tools can help content authors identify unnecessary words in many languages, including Arabic, English, Hindi, Mandarin, and Russian.
:::

exceptWhen:
• text content is:
    • poetic,
    • scriptural,
    • artistic, or
    • expressive rather than informational.
notes: Automated tools can help content authors identify unnecessary words in many languages, including Arabic, English, Hindi, Mandarin, and Russian.
examples:
• redundant modifiers such as ‘free gift’ and ‘past history’
  • double negatives to express a positive such as ‘She didn’t see nothing’ (which can be shortened to ‘She saw nothing’)
  • indirect phrasing such as ‘at this point in time’ (which can be shortened to ‘now’)
  • noun versions of verbs, such as ‘take into consideration’ (which can be shortened to ‘consider’)
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each sentence:

  1. Identify any words that may be unnecessary.
  2. Remove or replace the phrase with a simpler alternative.
  3. Check that no meaning is lost.
  4. Check that a technology in the accessibility support set meets ‘No unnecessary words.’

Expected results

  • #3 or #4 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: No Unnecessary Words: Sentences do not include unnecessary words.

title: Non-literal language explained
rawBody:
Explanations or unambiguous alternatives are available in text content for non-literal language, such as idioms and metaphors.

:::except-when
* text content is:
  * poetic,
  * scriptural,
  * artistic, or
  * expressive rather than informational.
:::

:::ednote
Translation software and other tools can aid content authors in identifying non-literal language.
:::

exceptWhen:
• text content is:
    • poetic,
    • scriptural,
    • artistic, or
    • expressive rather than informational.
editorNotes: Translation software and other tools can aid content authors in identifying non-literal language.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each phrase of non-literal language in text content:

  1. Check that access is provided to an unambiguous alternative or to an explanation of the non-literal text.
  2. Check that the non-literal text is presented in a way that is available to user agents, including assistive technologies (AT).
  3. Check that the accessibility support set meets ‘Non-literal language explained’.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true, or
  • #3 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Non-literal language explained: Explanations or unambiguous alternatives are available in text content for non-literal language, such as idioms and metaphors.

title: Numerical Alternatives Available
rawBody:
Explanations or alternatives are provided for complex numerical information such as statistics.

:::note
Complex numerical information can increase cognitive load, especially for users with a limited ability to understand and work with numbers. Providing written explanations or visualizations can aid understanding.
:::

:::example
Instead of:

> "The stadium holds 60,000 people."

Use:

> "The stadium holds 60,000 people, which is about the size of a small city."

Or:

> "The stadium holds many people."
:::

notes: Complex numerical information can increase cognitive load, especially for users with a limited ability to understand and work with numbers. Providing written explanations or visualizations can aid understanding.

“The stadium holds many people.”

Procedure

For any complex numerical information in the content:

  1. Check that an alternative is available that is not presented as complex numerical information.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

title: Summaries Available
rawBody:
A summary is available for long-form text content and:
* is identifiable visually and programmatically,
* uses concise sentences, and
* provides access to explanations of any uncommon words that are used in the summary.

:::ednote

Research is needed to determine the number of words that trigger the summary requirement and whether this threshold varies for different languages. If you are aware of research in this area, please email public-agwg-comments@w3.org.
:::

:::applies-when
* a page/view with continuous long-form text content that is organized in paragraphs and has 300 or more words.
:::

:::except-when
* long-form text content continues on multiple pages/views, only the first page/view requires a summary.
:::

appliesWhen: • a page/view with continuous long-form text content that is organized in paragraphs and has 300 or more words.
exceptWhen: • long-form text content continues on multiple pages/views, only the first page/view requires a summary.
editorNotes: Research is needed to determine the number of words that trigger the summary requirement and whether this threshold varies for different languages. If you are aware of research in this area, please email public-agwg-comments@w3.org.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For long-form text content that has 300 or more words:

  1. Check that a summary is present.
  2. Check that the summary can be identified visually and programmatically.
  3. Check that the summary explains uncommon words and uses concise sentences.

Expected results

  • #1, #2, and #3 are true.

plainEnglish.summary:
Summaries Available: A summary is available for long-form text content and:
 is identifiable visually and programmatically,
 uses concise sentences, and
 provides access to explanations of any uncommon words that are used in the summary.

title: Visual Aids Review
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

Visual Aids Review: [Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

 Our organization has a process and policy for reviewing text content to identify complex ideas such as processes, workflows, relationships, or chronological information, and adding visual aids to help readers understand them.

title: Text Color Adjustable
rawBody:
The foreground and background color of text can be adjusted without losing content or functionality.

A separate requirement may be needed if red/green color vision deficiency (CVD) is not accounted for within the contrast algorithm.
:::

appliesWhen: • text is presented, including text embedded in an image format.
exceptWhen:
• the text is:
    • also present elsewhere in the page/view which meets the requirement
    • part of an inactive interactive element
    • pure decoration
    • not visible to anyone
    • part of a picture that includes significant other visual content
    • part of a logo or brand name
notes: Transparency can cause testing issues, but should be tested as the rendered color.
editorNotes:
The contrast algorithm used in WCAG 3 is yet to be determined. For this draft, the requirement assumes the algorithm will include a size/weight factor. If the algorithm does not include size/weight, it will need to be added to this requirement text.

A separate requirement may be needed if red/green color vision deficiency (CVD) is not accounted for within the contrast algorithm.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each foreground and background combination of text:

  1. Identify the foreground color.
  2. Identify the background color.
  3. Check the contrast of text meets the [TBD algorithm].

Expected results

  • #3 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Text must maintain strong visual contrast against its background so it can be easily read by everyone, including people with low vision or under bright light.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Faint or low-contrast text forces users to strain their eyes and makes reading impossible for low-vision users.
plainEnglish.realWorldExample: Dark grey text (#333333) on a white background (#ffffff) provides a high 12.6:1 contrast ratio.

personaBreakdown.designer: Test all typography colors against backgrounds using APCA and WCAG contrast tools.
personaBreakdown.developer: Ensure CSS custom properties enforce compliant foreground and background hex values.
personaBreakdown.qa: Audit text elements across light and dark themes using Chrome DevTools Color Picker.
personaBreakdown.productManager: Reject brand color choices that cause accessibility failures.

statusSummary.workingGroupDebate: W3C working group is transitioning from WCAG 2 ratio formulas to APCA (Advanced Perceptual Contrast Algorithm) for better perceptual accuracy.
statusSummary.keyChallenges: Balancing dark mode aesthetics with high perceptual readability.

testingGuide.automated: axe-core color contrast audit; Lighthouse contrast test.
testingGuide.manualKeyboard: Inspect text readability across viewport zoom levels (up to 400%).
testingGuide.screenReader: Visual readability check for sighted screen reader users.

wcag22Comparison.deltaExplanation: WCAG 3 incorporates visual context (font weight, spatial frequency, ambient light) rather than fixed static ratios.

title: Text Customizations Retained
rawBody:
Content that is exported, saved, or printed retains user-applied text-appearance customizations.

:::applies-when
* the page/view can be exported, saved, or printed.
:::

:::example
Examples of interoperable formats
* PDF
* HTML
* SVG
* OpenDocument
:::

:::example
Examples of non-interoperable formats
* Scriptable Network Graphics
* DOCX, unless you know your audience has the required software (for example, you’re writing internal documents for your company which provides employees with the necessary software)
* Java object code
:::

appliesWhen: • the page/view can be exported, saved, or printed.
examples:
Examples of interoperable formats

  • PDF
  • HTML
  • SVG
  • OpenDocument

  • Scriptable Network Graphics
  • DOCX, unless you know your audience has the required software (for example, you’re writing internal documents for your company which provides employees with the necessary software)
  • Java object code
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each page/view:

  1. Adjust aspects of the text appearance, such as size, style, and color.
  2. Export, save, and print the content.
  3. Check that the customizations in #1 remain intact in the exported/saved/printed version. If there are multiple export options, check that at least one preserves the customizations.

Expected results

  • #3 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Text Customizations Retained: Content that is exported, saved, or printed retains user-applied text-appearance customizations.

title: Text Size Adjustable
rawBody:
Text can be increased in size to at least 200% of the platform’s default body-text size.

:::except-when
* the same text is available elsewhere in the page/view which can be increased to at least 200% of the platform’s default body-text size.
:::

exceptWhen: • the same text is available elsewhere in the page/view which can be increased to at least 200% of the platform’s default body-text size.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each block of text:

  1. Use each platform mechanism for increasing text size.
  2. Check that at least one mechanism can achieve a 200% text-size increase.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Text Size Adjustable: Text can be increased in size to at least 200% of the platform’s default body-text size.

title: Text Style Adjustable

Expected results

 text decoration
